title: The Throne verse, whole
tomorrow: finals, Dadi, Hana. is this more than one soul can carry?

cards: Somebody posts one line from a song, and the group chat splits in two: does she mean it literally, or is it a picture? Muslim scholars have had a gentle version of that argument, over one word in one verse.
The verse is the one Dadi says over Amira every night now that they share a hallway. Amira and her cousin Hana, still barely speaking about the bangles, have ended up arguing about the word instead.

teach.b: Weigh it first, phrase by phrase, in Pickthall's words. "Allah! There is no God save Him, the Alive, the Eternal. Neither slumber nor sleep overtaketh Him." No nap, no blink, no off switch.

All in the heavens and the earth is His; no one intercedes except by His leave; He knows what is before people and behind them. Then the line with the word: "His throne includeth the heavens and the earth."
Pickthall's throne is the Arabic kursi, and the verse is named for it: Ayat al-Kursi. So what is the kursi?
One reading, reported from Ibn Abbas and preferred by the commentator al-Tabari: the kursi is His knowledge, and His knowledge takes in the heavens and the earth. Nothing sits outside what He knows.

teach.h: KURSI AS REAL, WITHOUT ASKING HOW.
teach.b: The other reading, also handed down from early authorities: the kursi is real, a footstool distinct from the Throne, vast beyond picturing, affirmed as Allah describes it without asking how.
Here, scale is the point; we can't imagine it, and we aren't asked to.
Both readings meet in the verse's next words: "He is never weary of preserving them."
That's the line to tell a friend tonight: the Throne verse doesn't end on power. It ends on the absence of tiredness.

how: Muslims recite Ayat al-Kursi after the prescribed prayers and before sleep, and some parents and grandparents recite it over children at night.

o: Ayat al-Kursi, the verse of His all-holding kursi
the last verse of the Qur'an, about the Throne
the verse recited at a king's coronation

games.q: two readings of one word — tap the pairs.
p: of preserving the heavens and earth

s: the Throne verse pictures Allah resting after holding up the world
"Neither slumber nor sleep overtaketh Him" and "He is never weary of preserving them."
Muslim scholars have read the word kursi in more than one way
as His knowledge, reported from Ibn Abbas, or as a real footstool affirmed without asking how.

games.q: your study partner holds the footstool reading of the kursi; you lean toward knowledge. the teacher asks you to state her best case. what do you say?
o: it's handed down from early authorities, and it affirms what Allah says without asking how.
she just hasn't come across the knowledge reading yet, so she's working with less.
it was the only reading anyone held until modern scholars came up with another.
games.why: both readings are early. stating her best case honestly is part of reading the verse well.

practice: Copy one phrase of the verse by hand, slowly, on paper: neither slumber nor sleep overtaketh Him.
Then put the pen down and let your shoulders drop for the rest of the sit, the way tired people do when someone else is keeping watch.
